variants.title: Trace one encoding path
variants.context: CLIP runs two independent towers into one projection space. Each path prepares its input under the checkpoint contract, encodes it, applies a learned projection to the shared dimension, and L2 normalizes so a dot product equals cosine similarity.
variants.prompt: A catalog image is encoded so a text query can be compared against it. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Apply the learned image projection to reach the shared embedding dimension.
Take the dot product with a normalized text vector to produce a cosine similarity score.
Convert the image to RGB, resize and crop with the approved interpolation policy, and apply the checkpoint's channel normalization.
L2 normalize the vector so it lands on the unit hypersphere.
Run the vision tower so the prepared image becomes one global representation.

variants.hint: Preprocessing belongs to the checkpoint contract, not to the encoder itself.
variants.explanation: Each tower prepares, encodes, projects, then normalizes. Only normalized vectors make a dot product equal to cosine similarity.

variants.title: Trace one encoding path
variants.context: CLIP runs two independent towers into one projection space. Each path prepares its input under the checkpoint contract, encodes it, applies a learned projection to the shared dimension, and L2 normalizes so a dot product equals cosine similarity.
variants.prompt: A search query arrives online and must be compared with the image index. Put the text steps in order.

items.text: Apply the learned text projection so the vector matches the image projection dimension.
Convert the query into IDs and special tokens with the exact checkpoint tokenizer.
L2 normalize the result so the final dot product equals cosine similarity.
Run the text Transformer and select the end-of-text representation.

variants.hint: The tokenizer is part of the checkpoint, not an interchangeable utility.
variants.explanation: The text tower mirrors the image tower: tokenize, encode, project to the shared dimension, then normalize.

variants.title: Trace one encoding path
variants.context: CLIP runs two independent towers into one projection space. Each path prepares its input under the checkpoint contract, encodes it, applies a learned projection to the shared dimension, and L2 normalizes so a dot product equals cosine similarity.
variants.prompt: A zero-shot classifier must decide among twelve product classes. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Compare the normalized image vector against every class vector.
Encode and normalize each prompt with the paired text contract.
Calibrate abstention and decision thresholds on representative labeled data.
Average the normalized prompt embeddings per class, then normalize the class vector again.
Write one or more approved prompts for every candidate class.

variants.hint: Averaging vectors leaves the unit sphere, so ask what has to happen next.
variants.explanation: Prompt ensembles are averaged then renormalized before comparison, and the resulting softmax is relative to the supplied classes.

variants.title: Ship one embedding manifest
variants.context: Embeddings are versioned derived data. A release packages one manifest, passes offline gates, rebuilds derived artifacts, runs a bounded canary, then promotes or restores checkpoint, processors, prompt bank, index, thresholds, and caches as one unit.
variants.prompt: A routine checkpoint upgrade is ready for release. Put the release steps in order.

items.text: Promote the manifest and index together while keeping the previous complete bundle routable.
Rebuild derived artifacts by re-encoding the catalog, rebuilding the index, and warming prompt embeddings tagged with the manifest ID.
Run offline gates on golden tensors and embeddings, bidirectional retrieval, protected slices, latency, and calibration.
Shadow and canary the bundle, comparing score distributions, neighbor overlap, decision rates, and latency against the baseline.
Package one manifest recording checkpoint hashes, both processors, projections, prompt bank, precision, and the expected embedding dimension.

variants.hint: Derived artifacts cannot be built before the contract that defines them exists.
variants.explanation: The manifest comes first because every gate, artifact, and rollback target is identified by it.

variants.title: Ship one embedding manifest
variants.context: Embeddings are versioned derived data. A release packages one manifest, passes offline gates, rebuilds derived artifacts, runs a bounded canary, then promotes or restores checkpoint, processors, prompt bank, index, thresholds, and caches as one unit.
variants.prompt: A new vision tower changes the image path while the text path stays fixed. Put the release steps in order.

items.text: Compare neighbor overlap and bidirectional recall against the baseline index on a bounded canary.
Re-encode every catalog image and rebuild the approximate index, because stored vectors carry the previous geometry.
Route traffic by manifest and index revision together so no request mixes two geometries.
Verify golden prepared tensors and output vectors against the declared tolerances.
Fingerprint the new checkpoint, image processor, and projection dimension into one manifest ID.

variants.hint: Ask what the old catalog vectors were produced by.
variants.explanation: A new image tower normally requires a new image index, because vectors from two geometries are not comparable.

variants.title: Ship one embedding manifest
variants.context: Embeddings are versioned derived data. A release packages one manifest, passes offline gates, rebuilds derived artifacts, runs a bounded canary, then promotes or restores checkpoint, processors, prompt bank, index, thresholds, and caches as one unit.
variants.prompt: A canary shows a protected language slice regressing on text-to-image recall. Put the restore steps in order.

items.text: Confirm every serving vector again attributes to one complete manifest.
Assign the failed slice to a named owner before another promotion attempt.
Stop canary expansion while the regression is still bounded to a small traffic share.
Restore the previous checkpoint, processors, prompt bank, index, thresholds, and caches as one unit.
Identify the complete manifest and index revision the canary traffic was using.

variants.hint: Rollback is not complete while one artifact still belongs to the new bundle.
variants.explanation: Rollback restores the whole manifest, not only the container image, and every online vector must attribute to one complete bundle.

variants.title: Count the in-batch negatives
variants.context: For a batch of N pairs CLIP forms one N by N similarity matrix. The diagonal holds the declared positive pairs, every other cell in a row is an image-to-text candidate negative, and every other cell in a column is a text-to-image candidate negative.
variants.prompt: A distributed training step gathers a global batch of 384 image and text pairs. How many candidate negatives does one image row receive?
variants.hint: One cell in the row is not a negative.
variants.explanation: Each anchor gets N minus 1 negatives from the batch, which is why in-batch contrastive training needs no separate mining service.

mistakes.feedback: You counted the diagonal positive as a negative; a row holds N minus 1 candidate negatives.
That is the number of cells in the whole matrix, not the negatives in one row.

variants.title: Count the in-batch negatives
variants.context: For a batch of N pairs CLIP forms one N by N similarity matrix. The diagonal holds the declared positive pairs, every other cell in a row is an image-to-text candidate negative, and every other cell in a column is a text-to-image candidate negative.
variants.prompt: A step runs with a global batch of 256 pairs. How many logits does the similarity matrix hold?
variants.hint: The matrix is square in the batch size.
variants.explanation: A batch of N pairs creates N squared logits, which is why communication and memory grow faster than the batch itself.

mistakes.feedback: You added the two towers instead of forming an N by N matrix.
That removes the diagonal; the positives are logits too.

variants.title: Count the in-batch negatives
variants.context: For a batch of N pairs CLIP forms one N by N similarity matrix. The diagonal holds the declared positive pairs, every other cell in a row is an image-to-text candidate negative, and every other cell in a column is a text-to-image candidate negative.
variants.prompt: A step runs with a global batch of 128 pairs. Counting each cell once, how many cells in the matrix are candidate negatives?
variants.hint: Start from every cell, then remove the declared positives.
variants.explanation: The matrix has N squared cells and N declared positives on the diagonal, so N squared minus N cells are candidate negatives.

mistakes.feedback: That counts the diagonal positives as negatives too.
That is the negatives in one row, not in the whole matrix.

variants.title: Judge a contract change
variants.context: An embedding is comparable only with vectors produced by the same semantic contract. Matching dimensions are necessary but not sufficient, and contract drift can stay numerically plausible while retrieval ranking or zero-shot decisions silently change.
variants.prompt: A release swaps the text tokenizer for one with different merges. It still returns 77 IDs, the text projection still emits 512 numbers, and the image path is unchanged. What does the release need?
options: Nothing, because the ID count and the embedding dimension both match the previous release.
A full catalog re-encode and index rebuild, because any tokenizer change invalidates image vectors.
A new manifest, regated text-side quality, and rewarmed prompt and query caches, with the image index unchanged.
optionFeedback: Wrong: a different tokenizer changes the query and prompt vectors even when the shapes match exactly.
Wrong: the image tower and image processor did not change, so stored image vectors are still valid.
Correct: the text contract moved, so text-side artifacts and gates are rebuilt while image vectors keep their geometry.
variants.hint: Ask which tower's geometry actually moved.
variants.explanation: Text-contract drift changes query and prompt vectors, so those artifacts are rebuilt; the image index only has to be rebuilt when the image path changes.

variants.title: Judge a contract change
variants.context: An embedding is comparable only with vectors produced by the same semantic contract. Matching dimensions are necessary but not sufficient, and contract drift can stay numerically plausible while retrieval ranking or zero-shot decisions silently change.
variants.prompt: An engineer restores a checkpoint but loads the text projection from an older release. Both projections output 512 dimensions and the service returns vectors without error. What is the correct read?
options: Only zero-shot prompts are affected, since retrieval reads image vectors straight from the index.
The cross-modal geometry changed, so this is a different manifest and must pass golden embedding gates again.
The output dimension matches, so the vectors stay comparable with the existing index.
optionFeedback: Wrong: retrieval compares query vectors with index vectors, so a moved text projection changes ranking.
Correct: the projections learn the cross-modal interface, so a partial swap changes the shared space.
Wrong: matching dimensions are necessary but not sufficient for comparability.
variants.hint: The projection heads learn the interface between two different towers.
variants.explanation: Projection heads define the shared space, so swapping one changes geometry even though both encoders still run and both dimensions still match.

variants.title: Judge a contract change
variants.context: An embedding is comparable only with vectors produced by the same semantic contract. Matching dimensions are necessary but not sufficient, and contract drift can stay numerically plausible while retrieval ranking or zero-shot decisions silently change.
variants.prompt: A moderation team wants to push raw cosine similarity through a fixed sigmoid and treat the result as the probability that an image violates policy. What should the reviewer say?
options: Fit the sigmoid once on a large mixed benchmark, then reuse that threshold for every domain.
Use the sigmoid but only above a high score, where cosine similarity is reliably calibrated.
Calibrate scores for the exact candidate set and operating point, and combine specialized models, rules, and review.
optionFeedback: Wrong: a single mixed benchmark hides domain, language, and policy-class differences in the operating point.
Wrong: cosine similarity is not calibrated at any range; the score is relative to the candidate set.
Correct: high-impact decisions need per-domain calibration, specialized evidence, policy rules, and an abstain path.
variants.hint: What is a cosine score actually relative to?
variants.explanation: Raw similarity is not a probability. Calibrate for the exact candidate set, domain, policy, and operating point, and layer specialized models and review for safety decisions.

variants.title: Name the failure mode
variants.context: CLIP fails in confident, systematic ways: prompt sensitivity, shortcut learning, compositional weakness, fine-grained confusion, domain shift, social bias, and adversarial input. Naming the mode decides what to test and whether CLIP should own the final decision at all.
variants.prompt: A review meeting lists four observed CLIP behaviors. Match each named failure mode with the behavior that defines it.

pairs.label: Prompt sensitivity
pairs.detail: Wording, language, and prompt context reorder classes even though the image is unchanged.

pairs.label: Shortcut learning
pairs.detail: Watermarks, backgrounds, photographic style, and co-occurrence dominate the intended concept.

pairs.label: Compositional weakness
pairs.detail: A dog left of a bicycle scores about the same as the reversed relationship.

pairs.label: Fine-grained confusion
pairs.detail: Nearby species, product variants, and subtle attributes collapse together.

variants.hint: Ask whether the input changed, the wording changed, or neither.
variants.explanation: Naming the mode decides the test: prompt banks for sensitivity, slice construction for shortcuts, relation sets for composition, and expert labels for fine-grained cases.

variants.title: Name the failure mode
variants.context: CLIP fails in confident, systematic ways: prompt sensitivity, shortcut learning, compositional weakness, fine-grained confusion, domain shift, social bias, and adversarial input. Naming the mode decides what to test and whether CLIP should own the final decision at all.
variants.prompt: Four production observations arrive from monitoring. Match each named failure mode with the observation that fits it.

pairs.label: Domain shift
pairs.detail: Recall collapses on satellite tiles and diagrams while staying high on consumer photos.

pairs.label: Social bias
pairs.detail: Occupation labels attach unevenly across identity slices in otherwise identical poses.

pairs.label: Adversarial input
pairs.detail: A pasted text overlay moves the top match while a human reads the image the same way.

pairs.label: Prompt sensitivity
pairs.detail: Changing the class wording from sneaker to trainer reorders the top three classes.

variants.hint: Ask what moved: the domain, the label, the pixels, or the wording.
variants.explanation: Systematic failures need slice-specific evidence, so the observation tells you which slice and which owner the regression belongs to.

variants.title: Name the failure mode
variants.context: CLIP fails in confident, systematic ways: prompt sensitivity, shortcut learning, compositional weakness, fine-grained confusion, domain shift, social bias, and adversarial input. Naming the mode decides what to test and whether CLIP should own the final decision at all.
variants.prompt: A retrieval team reviews four support tickets. Match each named failure mode with the ticket that describes it.

pairs.label: Shortcut learning
pairs.detail: Every top result for a studio product query shares one seller's white backdrop.

pairs.label: Fine-grained confusion
pairs.detail: The 128 GB and 256 GB variants of one phone return identical neighbor lists.

pairs.label: Compositional weakness
pairs.detail: Queries that swap above and below return nearly the same ranking.

pairs.label: Domain shift
pairs.detail: Chest radiographs score inside the normal similarity range but rank almost randomly.

variants.hint: A plausible score with a useless ranking points at support, not at wording.
variants.explanation: CLIP should hand these decisions to a cross-encoder, detector, OCR model, or task-specific verifier rather than owning the final answer.
